samples.text:
The diagram shows how cement is produced and how it is used for making concrete. There are eight stages in the process.

First, limestone and clay are extracted from a quarry. Then the raw materials are crushed and mixed together. After that, the mixture is grinded into a fine powder. Next, the powder is heated in a rotating kiln to 1,450°C and it form clinker.

In the fifth stage, the clinker is cooled and grinded with gypsum, and this make cement. Then the cement is packed in bags, so it is ready to use.

After that, the cement is used to make a concrete. The concrete is made from 15% cement, 10% water, 25% sand and 50% gravel, so the gravel is the biggest part of the mixture. Finally, the concrete is poured into moulds and it is left to harden.

Overall, the process has two parts, the first part is producing cement and the second part is making concrete. It is interesting that the cement is only a small part of the concrete, although most of the stages are for making it.
samples.why: Overview at the end but identifies two parts · stages and percentages accurate · mechanical linking · adequate vocabulary · verb form and agreement errors plus a comma splice, meaning always clear.

samples.text:
The diagram illustrates the stages involved in manufacturing cement and the way in which this cement is then used to produce concrete.

Overall, the process has eight stages and can be divided into two parts: the first six stages concern cement production, while the last two show how concrete is made. It is also noticeable that cement makes up only a small proportion of the concrete.

The process begins with the quarrying of limestone and clay, which are crushed and mixed before being ground into a fine powder. This powder is heated to 1,450°C in a rotating kiln, forming a material called clinker. After it has cooled, the clinker is ground with gypsum to produce cement, which is then packed into bags.

To make concrete, the cement is combined with water, sand and gravel. Gravel accounts for the largest share at 50%, followed by sand at 25%, cement at 15% and water at 10%. In other words, gravel and sand together make up three quarters of the mixture. Finally, the concrete is poured into moulds, where it is leaving to harden into its final shape.
samples.why: Clear overview dividing the process into two parts · proportions accurately compared · logical progression with passives · some less common vocabulary (accounts for, proportion) · one minor verb form slip.

samples.text:
The diagram depicts the production of cement from raw materials and its subsequent use as an ingredient in concrete.

In total, there are eight stages, the first six of which relate to cement manufacture and the final two to the making of concrete. A striking feature is that cement, despite being the focus of most of the process, forms only a modest share of the finished concrete, which consists mainly of gravel and sand.

The raw materials, limestone and clay, are first quarried and then crushed and blended together. This mixture is ground into a fine powder and fed into a rotating kiln, where it is heated to 1,450°C to form clinker. Once cooled, the clinker is ground again, this time with gypsum, to produce cement, which is packed into bags.

In the concrete-making stage, the cement is combined with sand, gravel and water in fixed proportions. Gravel constitutes half of the mix and sand a quarter, while cement and water account for just 15% and 10% respectively. The concrete is then poured into moulds and left to set hard.
samples.why: Insightful overview linking cement production to its small share in concrete · figures used selectively and compared accurately · cohesion well managed · precise vocabulary · wide range of structures, error-free.
